hints: Look at Fig. 6.1 and separate the labels into two groups - P and O are control DNA sequences, while the three genes grouped together under one transcription arrow code for proteins.
Recall which three enzymes E. coli uses to take up and break down lactose - one splits lactose, one lets lactose into the cell, and one modifies lactose by-products.
walkthrough:
Spot the structural genes in the diagram**
In Fig. 6.1, P is the promoter and O is the operator. They do not code for protein, they are binding sites. The three genes transcribed together as one unit, lacZ, lacY and lacA, are the structural genes because they code for enzymes.

Match each gene to its enzyme**
lacZ codes for beta-galactosidase which hydrolyses lactose to glucose and galactose. lacY codes for lactose permease which transports lactose into the cell. lacA codes for transacetylase. Pick any two complete pairs for the table.
Final answer: lacZ - beta-galactosidase (lactase); lacY - lactose permease; lacA - transacetylase. Any two pairs for 2 marks.

hints: Think about the opposite of switching a gene on and off - if a cell leaves a gene switched on all the time, what must be true about how often it needs that protein?
walkthrough:
Why stay on all the time?**
Some proteins, like the lac repressor from gene I, respiratory enzymes or ribosomal proteins, are essential every minute. It would be wasteful and slow to keep switching them off and on. So their genes are transcribed constitutively to keep a constant supply available.
Final answer: The gene product / protein / enzyme is needed all the time / continuously by the cell.

hints: Start from gene I - it makes a protein all the time. Think where that protein goes to act in Fig. 6.1 when lactose is absent.
Think about what happens to RNA polymerase if that control site O is already occupied - can it still attach at P and move along lacZ, lacY and lacA?
walkthrough:
The repressor blocks the switch**
Gene I codes for the lac repressor protein. When lactose is absent, the repressor has the correct shape to bind tightly to the operator sequence O, which sits right next to the promoter P.

No transcription when blocked**
With the operator occupied, RNA polymerase cannot bind to the promoter or cannot move past it. So there is no transcription, no mRNA synthesis and no expression of lacZ, lacY and lacA. The operon is switched off.
Final answer: Repressor protein binds to the operator (O); blocks the promoter / prevents RNA polymerase binding to promoter, so no transcription of structural genes lacZ, lacY, lacA.

hints: Focus on the word inducible - it means something has to trigger or induce production. Think about what is newly present in the medium in part (b).
Link that trigger molecule to gene activity - what process from DNA to mRNA to enzyme is switched on only after the trigger appears?
walkthrough:
Made only on demand**
An inducible enzyme is not made all the time. The cell only makes it when the substrate it acts on is present. Here lactose acts as the inducer.

Inducer switches on the genes**
When lactose is present it binds to the repressor and changes its shape so it leaves the operator. This allows RNA polymerase to transcribe lacZ, lacY and lacA, so mRNA is made and the new lactose-metabolising enzymes are synthesised.
Final answer: Enzyme only produced when its substrate / inducer (lactose) is present; lactose causes gene activation / transcription / mRNA synthesis of the structural genes.

hints: Think about what making a protein costs a bacterial cell in materials and energy, and whether that cost is worthwhile if there is no lactose to use.
walkthrough:
Saving resources by staying off**
Making mRNA and protein uses nucleotides, amino acids and large amounts of ATP for transcription and translation. If lactose is absent, making beta-galactosidase and permease would waste all of these with no benefit. Keeping the operon off conserves energy and materials for growth and reproduction.
Final answer: Avoids waste of resources / energy, e.g. amino acids, ATP, nucleotides, when enzymes are not needed.
